name: Great Mosque of Sulaymaniyah
description: The congregational mosque founded in 1784 and completed in 1785 by the Baban emir Ibrahim Pasha, founder of the city. It holds the tomb of the cleric Haji Kaka Ahmad, the shrine of Sheikh Mahmud Barzanji and a domed mausoleum of the Baban family. It was rebuilt to its original form by 2024.

sources.sourceName: Wikipedia — Great Mosque of Sulaymaniyah
PUKmedia — PUK President visits Great Mosque
Wikidata Q5989794 (coordinates)

name: Sara (Saray) Building and Fatima Khan Bathhouse
description: The Saray government building in the old centre, built in the Baban era and rebuilt in 1926, beside the former Sara Gate square (Saray Azadi). Excavations from September 2025 uncovered the Baban-period Fatima Khan bathhouse behind it, demolished in 1954.

sources.sourceName: PUKmedia, 14 September 2025 — Historic bathhouse unearthed at Sulaymaniyah Sara

name: Sulaymaniyah Museum
description: Iraq’s second-largest archaeological museum, opened in 1961, with collections from prehistory to the Ottoman period. Since 2019 a gallery has displayed the inscribed blocks of the Paikuli tower.

sources.sourceName: Wikipedia — Sulaymaniyah Museum
Wikidata Q19414891 (coordinates)

name: Jasana Cave
description: Caves in the Surdash area north-west of Sulaymaniyah where Sheikh Mahmud Barzanji moved his printing press in 1923; Kurdish newspapers were printed there. The caves later sheltered Peshmerga and are now visited as a historic site.

sources.sourceName: KurdShop — Jasana Cave, a shelter for Kurdish revolution and Kurdish journalism
Kurdish Academy — Printing in Iraq: the 1920–58 period

name: Darband-i Gawr Rock Relief
description: A very large relief of a triumphant ruler cut high into a limestone cliff in the Qara Dagh gorge of Darband-i Gawr (“Pagan’s Pass”). Once attributed to Naram-Sin of Akkad, it is now dated by style to the Third Dynasty of Ur, around 2090 BC.

sources.sourceName: Columbia University, Mapping Mesopotamian Monuments — Darband-i Gawr Relief
Wikidata Q108861369 (coordinates)

name: Dailaija Rock Relief (Darband-i Basara)
description: A small, worn relief on the north face of the Darband-i Basara gorge near Dailaija, 25 km east-south-east of Sulaymaniyah, dated to around 2000 BC and linked to the Lullubi.

sources.sourceName: Columbia University, Mapping Mesopotamian Monuments — Dailaija Relief
World History Encyclopedia — The Lullubian rock relief of Darband-i Basara

name: Darband-i Belula Rock Relief
description: An Old Babylonian relief with a cuneiform inscription high on a gorge cliff near Belula, by the Iranian border, showing an armed man standing over two smaller victims.

sources.sourceName: Columbia University, Mapping Mesopotamian Monuments — Darband-i Balula Relief
Wikidata Q108861386 (coordinates)

name: Paikuli Tower and Inscription
description: A Sasanian victory monument of Narseh (r. 293–303) near Barkal village, with a bilingual Parthian and Middle Persian inscription telling how he overthrew Bahram III. The inscribed blocks are now in the Sulaymaniyah Museum.

sources.sourceName: Wikipedia — Paikuli inscription
Columbia University, Mapping Mesopotamian Monuments — Paikuli Monument

name: Qizqapan Rock-cut Tomb
description: An elaborately carved rock-cut tomb about 1 km west of Zarzi village, called Ishkewt-i Qizqapan (“Cave of the Ravisher”), probably for a local ruler of the Achaemenid or late Median period.

sources.sourceName: Columbia University, Mapping Mesopotamian Monuments — Qyzqapan Tomb

name: Kur u Kich Rock-cut Tomb
description: An apparently unfinished rock-cut tomb (“Cave of the Boy and Girl”) on the Banzad cliffs near Shornakh, 2–3 km south of Qizqapan; one of only two such tombs in Iraqi Kurdistan.

sources.sourceName: Columbia University, Mapping Mesopotamian Monuments — Kur u Kich Tomb

name: Zarzi Rock Shelter
description: A rock shelter near Chamirezan that gave its name to the Zarzian Epipalaeolithic culture of the Zagros.

name: Hazar Merd Caves

name: Kani Shaie
description: A mound in the Bazian basin 23 km west of Sulaymaniyah occupied from about 5000 to 2500 BC. Since 2013 a Coimbra–Cambridge–Slemani team has found an Uruk-period public building with wall-cone mosaics, cylinder seals and a gold pendant fragment.

name: Tell Kunara
